W hat is the most likely primary diagnosis?
Myxoedema coma may develop following a long history of
undiagnosed hypothyroidism or may occur in a patient with known
hypothyroidism with an additional decompensating event such as
infection or surgery. The clues in this scenario that point to this
diagnosis are the scar on her neck which could be a thyroidectomy scar
(which would mean the patient is likely to have hypothyroidism) and
the report of a productive cough 3 days before the admission. The
other clinical signs are consistent with myxoedema coma, including
type II respiratory failure, hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia,
tissue oedema and reduced Glasgow Coma Score (GCS). In severe
hypothyroidism, it is common to find hyponatraemia and
The past medical history of asthma, for which it is possible that the
patient takes a long-term steroid inhaler, coupled with the
presentations of hypotension and hypoglycaemia are consistent with
an adrenal crisis. However, this diagnosis does not explain the
impaired level of consciousness or the facial oedema. It is possible to
have adrenal insufficiency in addition to myxoedema coma, but the
Serotonin syndrome ought to be considered as the patient has a
history of depression, and therefore, it is possible that she takes a
medication that raises the level of serotonin. While serotonin
syndrome can cause impaired consciousness, the other clinical findings
are not consistent with this diagnosis, as you would also expect
Subclinical hypothyroidism tends to be asymptomatic; this would,
therefore, not explain these clinical findings. In subclinical
hypothyroidism, the thyroid-stimulating hormone level is elevated, but
the thyroxine level is in the normal range.
In a thyroid storm, patients experience reduced consciousness but will
also have hyperthermia, tachycardia, diarrhoea and jaundice. These
signs do not typically occur in myxoedema coma.

A 29-year-old woman, who has a 10-month-old baby, presents with                          Difficulty: Easy
neck and throat pain over the area of her thyroid. She tells you that she
had a flu-like illness a week or so before the pain began. Her partner,                Peer Responses %
who also attends the appointment, tells you she has been nervous and
agitated over the past week. On examination, there is a mild diffuse
enlargement of the thyroid gland and it is tender to palpation. Her BP
is 141/82 mmHg, and her pulse is 85/min and regular at rest. She has
Radioiodine uptake on the isotope scan is decreased.
W hich of the following forms of thyroiditis is the most                         Management
De Quervain’s thyroiditis, also known as subacute thyroiditis, is
characterised by acute onset of thyroid tenderness after a short viral
illness, with raised ESR but negative anti-thyroid antibodies. It is
thought to be linked to a response to viral infection, although a range
of different viruses such as influenza and Coxsackie B have been
implemented in its development. The early stages are characterised by
a period of thyrotoxicosis, and radioisotope scanning reveals decreased
thyroid uptake. As the disease progresses, there are phases of
euthyroidism and hypothyroidism, followed by a period of recovery to a
euthyroid state once again. Management centres on controlling pain,
with either non-steroidals or corticosteroids, and managing the
symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, normally with beta blockade.
Riedel's thyroiditis, also known as chronic sclerosing thyroiditis, is a
rare, chronic inflammatory disease of the thyroid gland characterised
by a dense fibrosis that replaces normal thyroid parenchyma. The
fibrotic process invades adjacent structures of the neck and extends
beyond the thyroid capsule. This feature differentiates it from other
inflammatory or fibrotic disorders of the thyroid. Extension beyond the
thyroid also differentiates this from the fibrosing variant of Hashimoto
thyroiditis. This intense fibrosis leads to a ‘hard’ feel of the gland.
Hashimoto's thyroiditis, also known as chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis,
is an autoimmune disease in which the thyroid gland is gradually
destroyed . Early on there may be no symptoms . Over time the thyroid
may enlarge, forming a painless goitre. Some people eventually
develop hypothyroidism with its accompanying weight gain, feeling
tired, constipation, depression and general pains . The thyroid function
tests in this scenario are in keeping with thyrotoxicosis. It is very
unusual for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis to present with negative anti-TPO
antibodies. Neither is pain in the neck a feature of the disease.
Graves’ disease, also known as toxic diffuse goitre, is an autoimmune
disease characterised by hyperthyroidism due to circulating
autoantibodies. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins bind to and
activate thyrotropin receptors, causing the thyroid gland to grow and
the thyroid follicles to increase synthesis of thyroid hormone. Graves’
disease, along with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, is classified as an
autoimmune thyroid disorder. In some patients, Graves’ disease
represents part of more extensive autoimmune processes leading to
dysfunction of multiple organs (e.g. polyglandular autoimmune
syndromes). Graves’ disease is associated with pernicious anaemia,
vitiligo, diabetes mellitus type 1, autoimmune adrenal insufficiency,
systemic sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Sjögren syndrome, rheumatoid
arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus. Painful goitre or neck pain
with flu-like symptoms is not a characteristic of this condition.
The peak incidence for postpartum thyroiditis is at month 6 post-
delivery. There is an initial period of thyrotoxicosis, followed by
hypothyroidism, then recovery, although a significant percentage –
perhaps as high as 40% – eventually become permanently
hypothyroid. Flu-like symptoms are not a feature.
